links.detail: On 14 August 2020 Angola's Supreme Court convicted former governor Valter Filipe (eight years), BNA manager Samalia (five years), José Filomeno dos Santos (five years) and businessman Sebastião (six years) of embezzlement, fraud and influence peddling over an attempted illicit transfer of $500 million to a London account, which a British bank blocked. After the Constitutional Court annulled the ruling, the Supreme Court plenary confirmed the convictions in 2024.
links.src_t: Tribunal Supremo confirma condenações no caso '500 milhões' (Ver Angola / Lusa)

links.detail: In October 2011 RBA subsidiaries Securency and NPA pleaded guilty to conspiring to bribe foreign officials to win banknote business with note-issuing authorities of Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal; they paid proceeds-of-crime penalties of A$19.8 million and A$1.86 million and fines of A$480,000 and A$450,000. Securency's former CFO received a suspended six-month sentence for false accounting (2012) and agent Radius Christanto a suspended two-year sentence (2013).
links.src_t: Chronology: Events related to charges against Note Printing Australia and Securency (Reserve Bank of Australia)

links.detail: Former managers of OeBS, the OeNB's banknote printing subsidiary, were tried for paying kickbacks to the central banks of Azerbaijan (20% overcharge) and Syria (14%) to win banknote orders, with about €14 million paid. Seven defendants were convicted in October 2014; after a Supreme Court-ordered retrial, the Vienna court in February 2018 gave Wolf and Miller 18-month suspended terms and Meyer 21 months suspended, while former OeNB deputy governor Duchatczek was acquitted.
links.src_t: More lenient sentence in the second instance in OeBS bribery scandal (CoinsWeekly)

links.detail: Attackers used Bangladesh Bank's SWIFT access on the night of 4 February 2016 to steal reserves from its New York Fed account ($101 million per The Daily Star; $81 million extracted per Prothom Alo). The government inquiry committee's final report of 30 May 2016 hinted at involvement of central bank officials and, according to Prothom Alo, named employees for action; the report was never published and no one was punished as of 2019.
links.src_t: Govt probe hints at BB officials' links (The Daily Star)

links.detail: The Bank of England triggered a three-year extension of its polymer banknote contract with De La Rue, which had been due to end in 2025 (to 2028); notes printed at the Bank's Debden facility.

links.detail: The Central Bank of Kenya awarded the contract to print new-look currency (Sh18 billion) to De La Rue International, which operates the Ruaraka plant co-owned by the Kenyan government; De La Rue beat Giesecke & Devrient, Crane Currency and Oberthur Fiduciaire. Crane AB disputed the award before the procurement review board.
links.src_t: Business Daily Africa: CBK defends De La Rue new currency contract

links.detail: Crane AB (Sweden) challenged the Central Bank of Kenya's award of the new currency printing tender to De La Rue as irregular and non-transparent; CBK rejected the claims.
links.src_t: Business Daily Africa: CBK defends De La Rue new currency contract

links.detail: Crane AB printed Swedish banknotes at Tumba (bought from the Riksbank in 2002). On 19 June 2018 the Riksbank gave notice to terminate the contract because Crane was moving printing to Malta.
links.src_t: Riksbank press release: The Riksbank gives notice to terminate contract with Crane AB

links.detail: Sveriges Riksbank signed an agreement with De La Rue (announced 19 September 2018) to print Swedish banknotes for just over three years, replacing Crane.

links.detail: Crane printed Liberian dollar banknotes for the Central Bank of Liberia under two contracts totalling L$15 billion at a cost of US$15,331,689.20.
links.src_t: FrontPage Africa: Crane Currency Refutes Wrong Doing in L$16 Billion Saga

links.role: Bribery or misconduct with the bank
links.detail: Liberia's Presidential Investigation Team alleged Crane conspired with CBL officials to print L$18,151,000,000, beyond the contracted L$15 billion. Crane denied wrongdoing and kickbacks and said it had not been charged; the PIT report also named former CBL Governor Charles Sirleaf. This is an allegation, not a finding by a court.
links.src_t: FrontPage Africa: Crane Currency Refutes Wrong Doing in L$16 Billion Saga

links.detail: Goznak (Russian state printer) printed Libyan dinars for the parallel eastern Central Bank (Benghazi/Bayda), which is not internationally recognized; Reuters-cited Russian customs data showed 4.5 billion dinars shipped Feb-June 2019. Malta seized two containers on 1 November 2019, citing UN resolutions that recognize only the Tripoli government.
links.src_t: Middle East Institute (Jonathan M. Winer): Seized Russian-printed dinars...

links.detail: The MEI article states that the regular Libyan dinar notes are printed by Britain's De La Rue.

pats.title: New York and London banking axis
pats.summary: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York is formally owned by its member banks: at end-2018 Citibank held 42.8% of its stock, JPMorgan Chase 29.5% and HSBC's US bank 6.1%, the last with its ultimate parent in London. In the 1920s the partnership of Benjamin Strong (New York Fed) and Montagu Norman (Bank of England, earlier a partner at the merchant bank Brown Shipley) set much of the direction of world finance; in 1925 the New York Fed opened a $200 million gold credit for the Bank of England and J.P. Morgan & Co. a $100 million credit for the British government so that sterling could return to gold. The London houses Morgan Grenfell (half-owned by J.P. Morgan & Co. from 1910) and Brown Shipley (a branch of Brown Brothers until 1914) were London ends of New York banks, and J.P. Morgan & Co. led the American banking group that took the US share of the Bank for International Settlements in 1930. Since 31 October 2013 the Fed and the Bank of England have had a standing swap line.

pats.uncertain: Holding Reserve Bank stock is a condition of Fed membership and is not ordinary ownership: it cannot be sold or pledged and voting is limited to electing six of nine directors. Holder-level figures exist only for 2007 and 2018 (via FOIA). No primary source supports Mullins' claim that London merchant banks control the New York banks. The personal Strong-Norman tie is well documented, but how far it set Fed policy is debated by historians and is not settled here.
pats.implications: The bank that carries out US monetary policy is formally owned by the large commercial banks it supervises and rescues, two of which held nearly three-quarters of its stock in 2018. That stock does not give them control of interest rates, which are set by the Fed's Board and its rate committee, but it does give them seats in the room: they elect six of the New York Fed's nine directors. The 1920s record shows how much of the world's money was steered through a few personal and banking ties between New York and London, outside any vote. For an ordinary reader, the point is that the people closest to the money supply have long been bankers and their partners abroad, not the public. Whether that closeness bends policy today is argued, not proven. The claim that London's merchant banks secretly control the Fed rests on one author and no records.

pats.title: Basel and the central bankers' clubs
pats.summary: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) was set up in Basel in 1930 under the Young Plan to handle German reparations; its first capital came from five European central banks plus a Japanese banking group and an American group led by J.P. Morgan & Co., and its first president was Gates McGarrah, former chairman of the New York Fed. Under a 1987 agreement with Switzerland its premises and archives are inviolable, it is immune from Swiss courts and from seizure of its assets and of deposits placed with it, and it pays no Swiss taxes; it is audited by a private firm (PwC up to the year to March 2026), not by a national audit office. Around it sit the Basel Committee (1974), which writes the bank-capital rules its members commit to apply, the Financial Stability Board (1999/2009), the invitation-only Group of Thirty (1978), which seats serving central bankers beside private bankers, and the Kansas City Fed's Jackson Hole meeting (since 1982).

timeline.event: The Young Plan was adopted at the Hague Conference on 20 January 1930 and a convention establishing the BIS in Switzerland was signed the same day.
The BIS's first financial year began on 17 May 1930; its first annual report was signed by Gates W. McGarrah, President.
G10 central bank governors set up the Basel Committee at the end of 1974 after the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt.
The Group of Thirty was founded by Geoffrey Bell at the initiative of the Rockefeller Foundation, which gave initial funding.
The Kansas City Fed moved its symposium to Jackson Hole, a location chosen partly because Fed Chairman Paul Volcker liked fly fishing.
The Swiss Federal Council and the BIS signed the Headquarters Agreement in Bern on 10 February 1987 (immunity from jurisdiction and execution, inviolable archives, tax exemption).
The Basel Accord set a minimum ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets of 8%.
The Fed took up the two BIS board seats reserved for the US central bank, held by the Fed Chairman and the New York Fed President.
G7 finance ministers and governors founded the Financial Stability Forum, succeeded by the FSB in April 2009.
The European Ombudsman recommended on 15 January 2018 that Draghi suspend his G30 membership, calling the G30 a private, invitation-only body whose members include banks the ECB supervises.
PwC signed off the BIS accounts for the year to 31 March 2026, the seventh and final year of its term; Fabio Panetta began chairing the BIS Board on 3 June 2026.

pats.uncertain: Who funds the Group of Thirty today was not found in an opened source (Wikipedia gives only the Rockefeller Foundation start-up money and an FY2007 budget of $448k). Jackson Hole's funding and invitation rules were not found. The BIS is not exempt from audit: PwC audited it to March 2026, but no national audit office reviews it, and who appoints the auditor was not checked in an opened source.
pats.implications: Central bankers set much of their common direction in a few small rooms in Basel, Washington and Jackson Hole. Some, like the Group of Thirty, also seat private bankers. The BIS, owned by central banks, cannot be sued in Swiss courts, its assets cannot be seized, it pays no Swiss tax, and no national auditor reviews it. The bank-capital rules written in Basel are then copied into national laws that decide how much your bank can lend and what it must hold in reserve, yet no voter elects the people who draft them. These forums are not secret: their members and reports are public. What a reader cannot see is what is said inside, and who pays for some of them.

pats.title: France's franc zone in Africa
pats.summary: The CFA franc was created on 26 December 1945, the day France ratified Bretton Woods; its name first meant 'franc of the French Colonies of Africa'. The French Treasury guarantees unlimited convertibility at a fixed rate (now 1 euro = 655.957 CFA francs); in return the central banks kept operations accounts at the French Treasury and deposited part of their reserves there: the BEAC (Central Africa) at least 50% (65% before 2007) and the Comoros at least 65%, while the BCEAO (West Africa) deposited 50% until its account was closed in January 2020. France devalued the CFA franc by 50% on 12 January 1994 and paid the BCEAO about €40 million a year in interest on its deposits (2018-2019). Under the agreement of 21 December 2019 France left the West African bodies' boards, but it still guarantees the currency and the six Central African states and the Comoros remain under the old terms.

pats.uncertain: The total balances in the operations accounts were not found. Whether French administrators still sit on the BEAC and Comoros boards was not confirmed from a primary text (an EcoMatin article of March 2023 expects their 'gradual withdrawal' under a future reform). The 'eco' had not replaced the West African CFA franc in any source read.
pats.implications: Fourteen African countries and the Comoros use money whose exchange rate and convertibility are guaranteed by France's treasury, a former colonial power. For decades that came with a duty to park at least half their reserves in Paris, and French officials sat on their central banks' boards (in West Africa until 2019). When the currency's value was halved overnight in January 1994, the price of imports in CFA francs doubled for millions of people who had no say in the decision. West Africa won changes in 2019-2020, but the guarantee remains, and Central Africa and the Comoros still deposit reserves in Paris. The arrangement brings price stability, which supporters stress. It also means these countries' central banks cannot set their own money freely.

pats.title: Banknote printers bribing central banks
pats.summary: Banknote printers owned by central banks paid bribes to win note contracts from other central banks. Securency (50% owned by the Reserve Bank of Australia from 1996) and Note Printing Australia (an RBA branch, then RBA company from 1998) pleaded guilty in October 2011 to conspiring to bribe officials over notes for Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal between 1999 and 2004, and gave up A$19.8 million and A$1.9 million in proceeds. In Vienna, managers of OeBS, a 99.75% subsidiary of Austria's central bank, were convicted of padding contracts for the central banks of Azerbaijan (20%) and Syria (14%) and routing the excess back to local decision makers. The private British printer De La Rue was investigated by the UK Serious Fraud Office over South Sudan (2019-2020); the case was closed without charges.

pats.implications: Here central banks were on both sides of the bribe. Firms owned by the central banks of Australia and Austria paid officials at other central banks to win the contracts to print their national money. The client countries' citizens paid the inflated price through their own central banks, and in the Austrian cases the padding was 14-20%. The buyers' officials were almost never named or convicted, and no court found that the owners' boards knew. The pattern shows how the printing of money, which most people never think about, is a private contract market open to the same corruption as arms or construction deals.

pats.title: Wall Street and central bank revolving door
pats.summary: Many central bank chiefs came from, or went to, the same few private firms. Goldman Sachs alumni include Mario Draghi (Goldman International vice chairman 2002-2005, then Bank of Italy and ECB), Mark Carney (13 years at Goldman, then Bank of Canada and Bank of England), William Dudley (Goldman chief US economist, then New York Fed), Neel Kashkari (Minneapolis Fed) and Hafize Gaye Erkan (Türkiye, 2023); Robert Kaplan went from Goldman partner to the Dallas Fed and back to Goldman as vice chairman in 2024. Fed chairs and vice chairs came from Carlyle (Powell, Quarles), Morgan Stanley (Warsh, chair from May 2026) and Citigroup (Stanley Fischer, before the Bank of Israel). Exits run to BlackRock (Hildebrand, Fischer), Citadel and PIMCO (Bernanke), Warburg Pincus (Geithner), UBS (Weber), Commerzbank (Weidmann), Brookfield (Carney) and Goldman (Corrigan).

Friedman resigned over a share purchase; Kaplan resigned in 2021 after scrutiny of his trading, and the Fed Inspector General found an 'appearance' of acting on confidential FOMC information. Whether these career paths bend policy toward the firms involved is argued by critics but is not shown by any source read here.
pats.implications: Many of the people who set interest rates and supervise banks came from, or went on to, the same handful of firms: Goldman Sachs, Carlyle, Morgan Stanley, Citigroup, BlackRock, Citadel and PIMCO. Officials learn how markets think, and the firms gain people who know how regulators think and whom to call. No source here shows a decision bent for a former or future employer. The worry critics raise is quieter: when rule-makers share careers, contacts and assumptions with the industry they oversee, the industry's view of what is reasonable tends to become the official view. A reader should notice that ordinary depositors and borrowers have no similar path into these jobs.

pats.title: Frozen and seized central bank reserves
pats.summary: Central banks keep much of their reserves in New York, London and Brussels, which lets the US, UK and EU freeze them. The New York Fed held about 507,000 gold bars (6,331 tonnes) for governments and central banks in 2024 and $2.63 trillion of US Treasuries in custody for foreign official accounts in July 2026; the Bank of England holds about 400,000 bars and calls itself the second-largest gold custodian. The US froze Iran's central bank assets in 1979, more than $34 billion of Libyan government assets in 2011 and about $9.5 billion of Afghanistan's central bank in 2021; the Bank of England has withheld 31 tonnes of Venezuelan gold since 2019. After February 2022 Western states immobilised Russian central bank assets, about €185 billion of them at Euroclear in Brussels; the EU has sent their windfall profits to Ukraine since 2024 and in December 2025 froze them indefinitely and kept the right to use them to repay a €90 billion loan to Ukraine.

pats.implications: A country's savings held abroad are only as safe as its relations with the place that holds them. Because so many central banks keep gold and dollar assets at the New York Fed, the Bank of England and Euroclear in Brussels, the US, UK and EU can freeze them, and have done so to Iran, Libya, Afghanistan, Venezuela and Russia. Each freeze had a stated reason: hostage-taking, war or contested government. Each also showed every other country that its reserves can be used as leverage. In Afghanistan's case it left the central bank of a country already in crisis without most of its reserves.

pats.title: Fed swap club versus PBoC network
pats.summary: Swap lines let a central bank borrow another's currency in a crisis, and the Fed decides who can borrow dollars. In 2007-2008 it opened lines with 14 central banks, with use peaking at $583 billion on 17 December 2008, but left out Russia, Turkey, India, Chile, Hungary and Iceland; on 31 October 2013 it made lines with only five (ECB, Bank of England, Bank of Japan, Bank of Canada, SNB) standing, and gave nine others temporary lines again in March 2020. The People's Bank of China has built a rival yuan network with 32 countries and regions (as of 30 September 2025); a 2023 study counted more than $170 billion of PBoC swap-line drawings in rescue operations for 22 countries from 2000 to 2021.

pats.implications: In a crisis, a swap line decides which countries can get dollars quickly and which cannot. The Fed gives standing access to only five central banks, all close allies, and in 2008 it left out countries such as Russia, Turkey, India and Iceland. Those countries had to spend their own reserves or go to the IMF, which attaches conditions such as spending cuts and higher taxes. China now offers a rival network to 32 countries and regions, much of it drawn in rescues. The effect for ordinary people is that whether their country's currency collapses in a panic can depend on its diplomatic standing with Washington or Beijing, not only on its own choices.

pats.title: Gulf oil states pegged to the dollar
pats.summary: Five of the six Gulf Cooperation Council states fix their currencies to the US dollar: Saudi Arabia at 3.75 riyals since 1986, the UAE at 3.6725 dirhams (official since 1997), Qatar at 3.64 riyals, Oman and Bahrain; Kuwait switched to a basket in May 2007. In July 1974, after the oil embargo, US Treasury Secretary William Simon agreed in Jeddah that Saudi Arabia would put petrodollars into US Treasuries through special 'add-ons' outside public auctions, with its holdings kept secret; the US Treasury reported them only within an 'oil exporters' group for 41 years, until it disclosed about $117 billion in 2016. A US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation was set up at the same time to recycle petrodollars into US goods and services. The PBoC has since signed yuan swap lines with Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar.

After the 1974 oil embargo, Saudi oil earnings were recycled into US government debt under a deal kept secret for 41 years, and into US goods through a joint commission. The arrangement gave the US a steady buyer for its debt and gave the Saudi state security and market access, without public debate in either country. No source here shows a written promise to price oil only in dollars; that popular claim is unproven. The recent Chinese swap lines with the Gulf states show the arrangement is no longer the only option.

pats.title: Global wave of central bank independence laws
pats.summary: From 1989 country after country passed laws shielding central banks from governments. Chile (Law 18.840) and New Zealand (Reserve Bank Act) led in 1989; Garriga's dataset counts 343 country-year reforms raising independence from 1970 to 2023, 135 of them in 1989-1999, with peaks of 16-18 a year in 1991-1993 as post-socialist states wrote new laws and another in 1998 when euro members handed policy to the ECB. Studies tie the wave to outside pressure: reforms follow IMF loan programmes (Romelli 2022; Kern, Reinsberg and Rau-Göhring 2019, 124 countries 1980-2012), and EU treaty articles 130-131 require independence before euro entry. Since 2010 increases have slowed while reforms cutting independence continue (Garriga: 73 country-year decreases in all).

The ECB's June 2026 Convergence Report checks Czech, Hungarian, Polish, Romanian and Swedish central bank laws against Treaty Articles 130 and 131.

pats.uncertain: The datasets record laws, not practice: a law can raise formal independence while a government keeps control in fact. The IMF and EU links are statistical associations from the cited studies; which reforms were written as IMF loan conditions is not coded country by country here.
pats.implications: Most of the laws that now shield central banks from elected governments were passed in a single generation, 1989-1999. Many followed loans from the IMF or the conditions for joining the euro. The shield cuts both ways. It keeps politicians from printing money before elections, but it also moves decisions over jobs, prices and debt away from voters to appointed experts and the international bodies that encouraged the change. The laws record what is written, not what happens. The parallel wave of governor firings shows that governments still reach in when they want to.

pats.title: Waves of banking crises and rescues
pats.summary: Systemic banking crises, which central banks and treasuries end with liquidity loans and bailouts, come in waves. The IMF's Laeven-Valencia database (1970-2025) shows clusters in 1980-1983 (Latin America's debt crisis: Argentina, Chile, Mexico, Uruguay, Colombia, Ecuador), 1994-1995 (Mexico and a run of transition and African economies, 24 starts), 1997-1998 (Asia and Russia, 15 starts) and 2007-2008 (the US and UK, then 22 more, mostly in Europe). Fiscal costs reached 55.1% of GDP in Argentina (1980), 56.8% in Indonesia (1997), 43.8% in Thailand and 37.6% in Iceland and Ireland (2008). The map's own corruption file holds 15 cases where central banks are accused of hiding losses or rescuing failing banks.

After the US and UK (2007), 22 countries began systemic crises in 2008, the largest one-year count in the database.
Fed swap lines peaked at $583 billion on 17 December 2008.
Romelli finds financial crises are generally followed by reforms that reduce central bank independence.

pats.series_note: Count of crisis episodes by start year in Table A1 of IMF WP/26/094 as parsed into /root/cb/raw/lv_crises.json (164 episodes). Countries are assigned to the first of the four marked waves in which they had a crisis start; later starts are added to the note.
pats.uncertain: The database dates crises by when 'significant signs of distress and substantial policy interventions' appear; some fiscal costs are not reported. Waves show timing, not a single common cause.
pats.implications: Banking crises arrive in waves that cross borders: Latin America in the early 1980s, Asia in 1997, the US and Europe in 2008. In each wave, central banks lend heavily to failing banks and governments spend public money to rescue them, at a cost of up to 57% of a year's national output in Indonesia. Bank owners and creditors are often protected while taxpayers and depositors bear the losses. The map's cases include central banks accused of hiding losses or choosing which banks to save. The waves show that the rescue machinery is a standing feature of the system, not a one-off emergency.

pats.title: Governments removing central bank governors
pats.summary: Alongside the laws protecting central banks, governments keep removing or pressuring their governors. Türkiye's president replaced four governors by decree between July 2019 and June 2023, usually after disputes over interest rates; Nigeria, Zambia, Malawi, Iran, Libya, Sudan and Myanmar's junta removed governors in 2020-2025, and governors in Ukraine (2020) and Bangladesh (2024) resigned under pressure. In the US, President Trump announced the firing of Fed Governor Lisa Cook in August 2025 and the Justice Department served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas in January 2026; the Supreme Court let Cook stay on the board in June 2026. The legal record shows the same drift: Garriga codes 73 country-year reforms that lowered independence from 1970 to 2023; since 2000 there were 3 or more a year in 2003-2004, 2008, 2011 and 2018-2019.

pats.uncertain: No complete global register of governor dismissals was found; the counts from the map's events file cover only the cases collected there. The legal-index series end in 2023 and do not yet capture 2024-2026 changes.
pats.implications: Laws that make central banks independent do not stop leaders from firing or pressuring their governors when interest-rate decisions go against them. Türkiye replaced its governor four times between 2019 and 2023, during years of high inflation and a falling lira. The US case shows the same tension can reach the world's most important central bank. These removals are the visible part of political influence. The quieter part is that a governor who expects to be fired may decide differently before anyone says a word.

pats.title: Lebanon's central bank financial engineering
pats.summary: From 2015-2016 Banque du Liban (BdL) under Riad Salameh, governor for three decades until 2023, ran 'financial engineering': it gave commercial banks high returns to bring in dollar deposits from abroad and place them at the central bank, and paid premiums on government bonds. The Alvarez & Marsal forensic audit found BdL's foreign-currency position went from a $7.2 billion surplus at end-2015 to a $50.7 billion deficit at end-2020 with no loss shown on the balance sheet, Bank Audi and Blom Bank as the largest beneficiaries, and $111 million in commissions to unknown recipients; its 2018 accounts, signed with qualifications by EY and Deloitte, booked a $6.82 billion 'seigniorage' asset. Separately, about $330 million flowed in 2002-2015 through Forry Associates, a British Virgin Islands company owned by Salameh's brother, into property in France, Germany, Luxembourg and Belgium; the World Bank called the system 'Ponzi finance' in 2022 and the US, UK and Canada sanctioned Salameh in 2023.

pats.implications: Lebanon's central bank kept the country's money looking stable for years by paying banks high returns to bring in new dollar deposits, which were used to cover earlier promises. Its own accounts hid the losses behind an invented asset, and two of the world's largest audit firms signed them, with qualifications. When it broke, ordinary depositors lost access to their savings while the largest banks had been the largest beneficiaries. Separately, investigators say about $330 million moved through a company owned by the governor's brother in the British Virgin Islands. The case shows how a central bank can run a scheme the public cannot see until it fails, and how offshore shells and auditors can help it last.

pats.title: City of London and its offshore islands
pats.summary: London became the centre of offshore dollar banking in the late 1950s: after UK exchange controls of 1957 limited sterling lending to non-residents, London banks lent dollars instead, and Midland Bank bid for dollar deposits above the ceiling US rules (Regulation Q) allowed at home. The UK's overseas territories and Crown dependencies, which are not part of the UK but whose defence and foreign relations London handles, are among the largest secrecy jurisdictions: in the Tax Justice Network's 2025 Financial Secrecy Index the UK plus ten of them account for 9.26% of the global secrecy score, more than the United States alone (5.66%, rank 1). Two central bank cases in the map's files touch this network: Lebanon's Forry Associates was a British Virgin Islands company, and a Nigerian investigator said the CBN's former governor placed £543 million in UK fixed deposits without board approval.

pats.uncertain: The Financial Secrecy Index is built by an advocacy group from secrecy scores weighted by financial scale; a high share is not proof of illicit flows. The FSI covers 141 jurisdictions. How much central bank money passes through these jurisdictions was not measured in any source read.
pats.implications: London built the market where dollars are lent outside US rules, and the islands and territories that London represents abroad, such as the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Jersey and Guernsey, are among the world's main places to hide who owns money. Together the UK and ten of them make up more of the world's financial secrecy than the United States, the top-ranked single country. That matters to central banks because looted or bribed money, including in the Lebanese and Nigerian cases on this map, often passes through these places. For ordinary people it means tax and corruption losses in their own country can end up in accounts their governments cannot see into.

pats.title: Four firms auditing the central banks
pats.summary: Most central banks that hire private auditors use one of four firms. Of 28 institutions whose auditor the map has traced (27 central banks plus the BIS), PwC, EY, KPMG and Deloitte audit 17: PwC signs for six central banks and the BIS, EY for five (including the Bank of England), KPMG for the US Federal Reserve Banks, Spain and Switzerland, and Deloitte for France (with Mazars) and Türkiye; seven others (Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Sweden, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand) are audited by state audit offices instead. The same firms also appear in scandals: EY and Deloitte qualified but signed Lebanon's 2018 central bank accounts that carried a $6.82 billion invented asset.

pats.uncertain: The sample covers only the 28 institutions traced in networks.json; auditors of the Bank of Italy, Bank of Korea, Banco de México, Saudi Central Bank, Bank of Russia, PBoC and others were not found. Concentration among four firms is a feature of the whole audit market and is not proof of influence over central banks.
pats.implications: Most central banks that hire private auditors use the same four firms, which also audit the commercial banks those central banks supervise. An audit tells the public that the accounts are fair. When the same firms check both the rule-maker and those it rules, and sometimes sign off accounts that later prove misleading, as in Lebanon, the public's main independent check is less independent than it looks. Concentration in four firms is true of the whole audit market and is not proof of influence. It does mean a small number of private partnerships stand between central banks' books and the public.
